clinicalPearls: This rare ectodermal disorder combines vascularising keratitis, an ichthyosiform erythrokeratoderma and congenital sensorineural deafness.
It is usually caused by dominant gain-of-function variants in GJB2, the gene for connexin 26, most classically a specific recurrent substitution affecting the channel.
Unlike common recessive GJB2 deafness, the KID mutations act on the gap-junction hemichannel to produce a toxic gain of function affecting skin, cochlea and cornea.
The skin shows well-demarcated erythematous hyperkeratotic plaques with a characteristic stippled or leathery grainy surface, plus thickened palms and soles.
The keratitis is progressive and vascularising, causing photophobia, corneal neovascularisation and potential blindness rather than a simple dry-eye complaint.
Deafness is congenital, bilateral and profound, and cochlear implantation may be considered.
Patients are prone to recurrent mucocutaneous candidal and bacterial infection and to cicatricial alopecia and nail dystrophy.
There is a lifelong increased risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, warranting long-term skin surveillance.
reference.pathophysiology: Keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness syndrome is a connexin disorder caused predominantly by heterozygous missense variants in GJB2, which encodes connexin 26, a gap-junction protein that oligomerises into hexameric hemichannels (connexons) in the epidermis, cochlea and corneal epithelium. Whereas loss-of-function GJB2 variants cause common recessive non-syndromic deafness, the variants responsible for KID syndrome act through a dominant gain of function: they impair the normal gating of the hemichannel so that connexons remain aberrantly open at the plasma membrane, allowing pathological leak of ions and small molecules, cellular calcium dysregulation and disturbed intercellular communication. In the cochlea this disrupts potassium recycling through the supporting-cell gap-junction network needed to maintain endolymph and the endocochlear potential, producing profound congenital sensorineural deafness; in the epidermis it deranges keratinocyte differentiation and barrier formation, giving erythrokeratoderma, palmoplantar keratoderma and increased susceptibility to infection and malignant transformation; and in the avascular cornea it drives epithelial breakdown, neovascularisation and progressive keratitis. A minority of cases, particularly a more severe lethal neonatal form, arise from variants in GJB6 (connexin 30), reflecting the shared role of these connexins in the same tissues.
additionalDifferentials: Non-syndromic recessive GJB2 deafness without skin or eye disease
Other congenital ichthyoses such as ichthyosiform erythroderma and Netherton syndrome
Vohwinkel syndrome with palmoplantar keratoderma and deafness
Clouston hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (GJB6) with nail and hair changes
Hystrix-like ichthyosis with deafness, an allelic severe phenotype
Acquired vascularising keratitis and chronic ocular surface disease
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing of GJB2 and, where indicated, GJB6
Comprehensive audiometry and brainstem-evoked response testing
Slit-lamp ophthalmological assessment for keratitis and corneal neovascularisation
Skin biopsy and histopathology of hyperkeratotic plaques
Microbiological sampling for recurrent candidal and bacterial infection
Regular dermatological surveillance for squamous cell carcinoma
Family and pedigree evaluation given usually de novo dominant inheritance
redFlags: Progressive corneal neovascularisation and visual deterioration despite ocular lubrication
New, enlarging or ulcerated skin lesion suggesting squamous cell carcinoma
Severe or systemic mucocutaneous infection in the neonatal or lethal variant
Profound congenital deafness delaying language acquisition
Extensive erythroderma with impaired thermoregulation and fluid loss in infancy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies with severity: many patients survive into adulthood with chronic skin, hearing and corneal morbidity, but the neonatal severe form carries high mortality from infection, and the lifelong risk of squamous cell carcinoma and progressive keratitis threatens both survival and sight.
pitfalls: Assuming any GJB2 variant is recessive and non-syndromic, thereby missing the dominant gain-of-function KID mutations
Managing the keratitis as ordinary dry eye and overlooking progressive neovascularisation
Failing to institute skin-cancer surveillance in a patient with chronic erythrokeratoderma
Attributing recurrent candidal infection to hygiene rather than the underlying barrier and immune defect
Overlooking hearing loss in a neonate whose skin disease dominates the presentation
management: Skin-directed therapy with emollients and keratolytics, and systemic retinoids such as acitretin for extensive erythrokeratoderma with treatment monitoring
Prompt antifungal and antibacterial treatment of recurrent candidal and bacterial skin infections
Ophthalmological care of the vascularising keratitis with ocular surface lubrication, topical therapy and corneal surgery where needed, plus photophobia management
Audiological rehabilitation including cochlear implantation for the profound congenital sensorineural deafness
Lifelong dermatological surveillance with biopsy of suspicious or non-healing lesions given the squamous cell carcinoma risk
Intensive infection control in the neonatal severe form, which carries high mortality
Clinical genetics referral and counselling for this dominant GJB2 (connexin 26) disorder, most cases arising de novo
